title: Workspace path boundary
pins: All 134 byte-exact path hazards, their stable refusal codes, and the platform-specific behaviour of an unguarded resolver. What a consumer loses if this drifts is the workspace boundary itself: a path the guard refuses in one language and resolves in another is a read or a write outside the workspace, reached through a service that believed it was protected. The refusal CODE matters as much as the refusal -- a consumer switches on it to tell a traversal attempt from an encoding problem from a device-name collision, and a code that differs by language collapses all three into an unknown failure. Paths are carried as base64 so invalid UTF-8 survives without being laundered through JSON, which is the same reason json-container-identity carries its boundary values as raw strings: the recording format must not repair the input the corpus is asking about.
scope: Path admission and its refusal code, across eight hazard families -- traversal, absolute paths, UNC, homoglyphs, device names, alternate data streams, encoding and raw bytes. It does NOT cover what happens to a path once admitted: no file is opened, no permission is checked, and the store behind the workspace is not exercised at all.
findings: All 134 rows agree across the three languages, which for a boundary this large is the result worth having -- and is still not the same as safety. Stated explicitly because this is the suite where `agrees: true` is most tempting to read as a guarantee: the corpus compares LANGUAGES, so any hazard none of the three refuses is invisible to it by construction. It confirms that a path refused by a PHP application is refused by a TypeScript or Python agent under the same code; it does not confirm that the hazard list is complete. New hazard families are added by writing rows, not by this run passing.
